vignette:
Elena, a 78-year-old librarian, still carries the night she fled Guatemala during the civil war. She and her husband slipped through a river while soldiers torched the village behind them. The damp earth and smoke filled her nostrils, and she left her younger brother hiding in the reeds-she never saw him again. The guilt settled in her chest that night and never left.

Now, decades later, the smells return without warning. When a library patron wears a musky cologne, Elena's nose catches that riverbank scent. Her eyes go wide, her shoulders tense, and she becomes hypervigilant-scanning the reading room for threats. She cannot focus on the book she is shelving; the letters blur. She has come to believe that only her small office and her home are safe, so she rushes through her tasks and retreats behind closed doors. To keep the dread at bay, she works hard at staying busy-accepting extra cataloging shifts, volunteering for inventory, anything to fill the hours. But when she finally stops, at night in her armchair, her mind starts to circle: Why did this happen to me? Why did I leave him? She repeatedly blames herself, going over every detail of that escape. The rumination pulls the smells back into the present-stronger now, with the guilt twisting through her stomach. And the more she replays the past, the more vigilant she becomes the next day, scanning every corner of the library as if the soldiers might step out from the stacks.

Elena cannot put the event into words. When her husband asks, she shakes her head-it comes only as odors and images. The intensity of the guilt when she recalls the riverbank makes her feel sick, and so she avoids speaking of it at all. Her concentration at work has become so poor that she misplaces books, and she has stopped visiting the market or the park. Only home and her office feel manageable. Her husband noticed she no longer attends their weekly card game with neighbors; she makes excuses about being tired. She keeps herself in constant motion during the day, but the cycle tightens: the hypervigilance feeds the need to stay busy, the busyness gives way to rumination, the rumination summons the smells, and the smells again set her on edge.

Last month, a colleague wore a floral perfume that unexpectedly mingled with the scent of old paper. Elena smelled smoke instead. She dropped a stack of books and began shaking, unable to explain why. That panic, and her growing fear that she is losing control, finally brought her to seek help. She is most afraid that the smells will never stop, and she hopes-quietly-that someone can help her find words for what she has carried alone for so long.
